summary: This document describes things IETF participants should consider when proposing new research groups in the IRTF. It emphasizes differences in expectations between the IETF and the IRTF.

plainLanguage.summary: One group builds standards, the other studies long-term ideas. This RFC explains to the first group how the second one works.

questions: how to start an irtf research group
what is the difference between irtf and ietf
how long does irtf research take
subtitle: Understanding how research groups differ from engineering groups

tldr.problem: IETF participants proposing new research groups to the IRTF often structure their proposals like IETF working groups, which is not what the IRTF is looking for.
tldr.mechanism: The IRTF prioritizes broad research exploration with longer timescales and multiple alternatives, while the IETF focuses on engineering consensus toward specific, interoperable standards.
tldr.outcome: Understanding these differences helps IETF participants propose research groups that fit the IRTF's mission and organizational culture.

today: RFC 7418 remains the standard reference for understanding how the IRTF differs from the IETF. It is an Informational RFC published in December 2014 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Understanding the Two Organizations
sections.content:
RFC 7418 is a guide for IETF participants who want to propose new research groups in the IRTF. Both organizations address problems in the Internet, but they approach them differently.

IETF participants tend to apply IETF practices when proposing IRTF research groups, which often leads to misunderstandings. This RFC describes the key differences so proposals can match what the IRTF actually needs.
sections.plainLanguage: IETF people know how to build things. IRTF people think about new ideas. The RFC tells IETF people how IRTF people work, so they can work together better.

sections.title: Research versus Engineering
sections.content:
The fundamental difference between the two organizations comes down to goals. Engineering aims for a finished product that works. Research aims for understanding and answering questions, even if those answers lead to new questions.

As Fred Baker notes in the RFC, "To me, the fundamental outcome of research is understanding, and the fundamental outcome of engineering is a product." A research group can succeed by opening new questions; an engineering group fails if it never finishes. Research can stay open-ended; engineering stops when the result is good enough to deploy.
sections.plainLanguage: Engineers finish things. Researchers ask questions. If an engineer keeps working forever, it is a problem. If a researcher keeps asking new questions, that is success.

sections.title: How IRTF Groups Operate
sections.content:
IRTF research groups operate in several ways that would be unusual for IETF working groups.

Scope: IRTF charters are broad. They describe a field of research rather than specific deliverables, and groups often shift focus over time as research interests change. IETF working groups have narrow, carefully constrained charters with specific milestones and deliverables.

Time and alternatives: IRTF groups plan to work on significant problems for at least three to five years. They actively explore multiple alternative approaches instead of converging on a single solution. IETF working groups use consensus to narrow choices and move toward one interoperable solution that can ship.

Process freedom: IRTF groups negotiate their own way of working and do not have to reach consensus like IETF groups. This flexibility lets them adapt to their research needs as the work evolves.
sections.plainLanguage: IRTF groups pick a big area to explore, work for years, and are OK with different ideas competing. IETF groups start with goals, work toward one answer, and ship when done.

sections.title: Deliverables and Completion
sections.content:
The two organizations also differ in what they expect groups to produce and when they finish.

IRTF research groups have no requirement to publish RFCs. They may produce IRTF-stream RFCs, Internet-Drafts for later IETF standardization, white papers, academic journal articles, or even just influence the research community through discussion. Success means stimulating discussion, producing relevant outputs, and impacting the field.

IETF working groups are typically chartered to deliver Internet standards. Their deliverables are protocols, deployment specifications, and operational guidance that can ship to the market.

Completion also differs: IRTF groups may pivot to better solutions partway through or continue research without a fixed end date. IETF working groups typically conclude when their chartered milestones are met.
sections.plainLanguage: IRTF groups can write papers, share ideas, or just teach others. IETF groups must build standards. IRTF groups might never finish; IETF groups wrap up when the job is done.

sections.title: Getting Started as an IRTF Research Group
sections.content:
For IETF participants proposing a new IRTF research group, the IRTF Chair recommends acting like an IRTF research group for a year first, to show the IRTF that the group can sustain research-focused work.

Concrete steps include recruiting a critical mass of researchers who can review and build on each other's work; identifying how the proposed group differs from other venues already working on the topic; holding workshops to survey existing work; and if the group expects to eventually feed results into IETF standardization, recruiting engineers to review progress.

However, proposing groups are not locked into these approaches. Emailing the IRTF Chair to start the conversation is a valid and reasonable strategy, since each proposed research group is different.
sections.plainLanguage: To start an IRTF group, get researchers together, study what others are doing, maybe hold a workshop, and show the IRTF Chair you can do research work for a year.
